I have farmed these lands in Quzhou County since I was a young boy following my father. I never went to school, but I know the soil here — it is heavy loam, good for grain, and the water table is deep but reachable by well. In our village, nobody questions the wheat-maize double crop. It is the only system that makes sense on the North China Plain. My 5 mu of land has grown wheat every winter for as long as I can remember, and maize every summer after the wheat comes off.

The wheat went into the ground last October after I rotary-tilled the field. I used improved wheat seed — about 30 jin per mu — bought from the dealer in town. I also spread basal compound fertilizer then. Now that spring has arrived and the wheat is greening up, my main job is to topdress with urea at the right time, irrigate when the soil dries, and watch for aphids. I will give the wheat two more irrigations after this green-up watering — one at jointing and one at grain filling — and spray insecticide twice plus herbicide once. I do not need a book to tell me when; I look at the crop and I talk to my neighbors.

As soon as the wheat is harvested in early June, I will plant hybrid maize the same day — there is no time to lose before the summer heat arrives. I use no-tillage now; everyone in the village plants directly into the wheat stubble because it saves diesel and days. I buy hybrid seed — Nongda 372 or something similar — about 1.5 packages per mu. I put down compound fertilizer at planting and topdress once when the maize is knee-high. Maize needs less water than wheat here; two good irrigations are usually enough, one at the big喇叭口 stage and one at filling. I spray herbicide once and insecticide twice. If the weather cooperates, I expect roughly 1000 jin of wheat per mu and 1100 jin of maize per mu. That is enough to feed my family and sell the rest.
